explain.headline: The Problem of Inflation and Second-Round Effects
static: Inflation refers to the general increase in prices and fall in the purchasing value of money over time, measured in India primarily through the Consumer Price Index and Wholesale Price Index.

Monetary Policy Committee is a statutory and institutionalized framework under the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, tasked with maintaining price stability while keeping in mind the objective of growth.
El Nino is a climate pattern that describes the unusual warming of surface waters in the eastern tropical Pacific Ocean, severely affecting Indian monsoons and agriculture.
Second-round effects of inflation occur when initial supply shocks or price hikes prompt workers to demand higher wages or firms to raise prices further, causing persistent inflation.
explain.what: The editorial discusses how rising global food and energy prices, coupled with El Nino threats to rabi crops, could intensify inflation and trigger second-round effects.
explain.why_in_news: Global food and energy prices are hardening amid a strengthening El Nino, raising concerns over economic policy tightening.
explain.background: Supply-side pressures from food and high crude oil prices can escalate core inflation and second-round price embedding if not managed by central bank policies.
significance: Highlights the vulnerability of Indian agriculture and rabi crops to climate phenomena like El Nino.
Outlines the key determinants for future monetary policy tightening by the central bank.
Emphasizes the danger of second-round price effects in sustaining broader inflationary pressures.
prelims: Brent crude oil is trading at around $115 per barrel according to the text.
Global food prices are hardening with potential momentum from a strengthening El Nino.
El Nino could potentially impact rabi crops in India.
explain.mains: Analyze the impact of global supply-side shocks and weather anomalies like El Nino on India's inflation trajectory and monetary policy response. (15 Marks)
explain.who: Central bank
explain.video_query: inflation second round effects and el nino impact india

stories.ai_why: Inflation dynamics and second-round effects are important for GS3 economy.

points: Price pressures are likely to intensify globally and domestically.
Global food prices are hardening, driven further by a strengthening El Nino.
Rabi crops in India face potential negative impacts from El Nino.
Energy prices remain elevated with Brent crude trading at around $115 per barrel.
The central bank previously noted limited signs of supply-side pressures embedding in pricing behavior.
Future policy tightening depends on committee assessments of supply-side pressures, growth-inflation dynamics, and second-round effects.
sum.text:
Price pressures are likely to intensify. Global food prices, which were relatively soft compared to energy and metals, are now hardening. This could gather further momentum with El Niño strengthening and possibly impacting rabi crops in India. Energy prices are also elevated — Brent crude oil is trading at around $115 per barrel. So far, the central bank has noted that there “are only limited signs of supply-side pressures getting embedded in pricing behaviour”. Going forward, the extent of policy tightening will depend on how committee members assess supply-side pressures across the economy, whether second-round effects take hold, and how growth-inflation dynamics evolve.

The central question is whether leadership change will alter Israel's political trajectory or escalate the ongoing conflicts with Gaza and Iran.
Opinion polls indicate neither the current coalition nor opposition parties will attain a majority, making the outcome dependent on shifting coalitions.
Netanyahu faces a close contest with Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party, who is a military veteran critical of Netanyahu's governance.
Naftali Bennett is also in the race, though coalition formation with right-wing parties remains fundamental for any government.
Netanyahu faces domestic blame for perpetual war, international isolation, and failing to dismantle Iran's nuclear enrichment programme.
Military operations in Gaza under Netanyahu have caused about 74,000 deaths and severe humanitarian crises, shifting blame onto him.

Regardless of election outcomes, major Israeli parties oppose a two-state solution, ensuring security and regional policies will likely remain unaltered.
sum.text:
Israel’s parliamentary election on October 27 will decide the fate of incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu .
It is significant because this is the first election since Hamas’s attack on Israel on October 7, 2023. The central question is whether a change in leadership will occur, and if so, whether it will usher in a new political trajectory. Many fear that a Netanyahu victory will embolden him to escalate the war against Iran and continue his coercive policies towards Gaza.
Given the fractious nature of Israel’s politics and shifting coalitions, it is difficult to predict the outcome. Opinion polls suggest that neither the present coalition nor the opposition parties will attain a majority. Netanyahu is locked in a close contest with Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of a newly formed Yashar party.
Eisenkot draws his popularity from his long military service, family sacrifices, and widespread anti-Netanyahu sentiment. He lost his son, Gal Eisenkot, during a military operation in Gaza in 2023. Widely seen as a hawk, he served in Netanyahu’s emergency war cabinet in 2024 and later resigned over disagreements with respect to Gaza. Thus, if he wins, expecting a moderation of Israel's policy would be premature.
Naftali Bennett, the former prime minister, is also in the race. However, much will depend upon the coalition that emerges, in which the support of right-wing parties would be fundamental.
The election is widely regarded as a referendum on Netanyahu's uncompromising and coercive approach to governance. He is being blamed for pushing Israel into a perpetual war with Iran and its proxies and for exposing the country to widespread international opprobrium and diplomatic isolation over its conduct in Gaza. He could neither topple the theocratic regime in Tehran nor succeed in destroying its nuclear enrichment programme.
Further, his military operations in Gaza have created the worst humanitarian crisis in recent years, leading to about 74,000 deaths. The disproportionate Israeli military response in Gaza shifted the narrative from attributing responsibility to Hamas to holding Netanyahu responsible for its escalation.
Netanyahu’s biggest success lies in convincing the Trump administration to launch a joint attack on Iran. In return, Trump has endorsed his leadership in the current election, praising him as an ally, a “great warrior prime minister”, and a peace partner. points: Armenia is hosting the COP17 biodiversity conference despite ranking poorly on waste management at 164th and wastewater treatment at 165th.
The author argues that Armenia has failed to use the hosting opportunity to address its longstanding and serious environmental challenges.
Armenia’s economy heavily relies on mining, including the Zangezur, Agarak, and Teghut copper-molybdenum mines using open-pit methods.
The World Bank identifies mining as a major pollution source, and the Artsvanik tailings reservoir is linked to heavy-metal waterway contamination.
Forests cover only 11.1 percent of Armenia, and Yerevan’s fine particle air pollution is five times WHO recommended limits.
Reliance on Russian-linked businesses controlling major operations like Zangezur gives the government economic incentives to protect polluting industries.
Days before COP17, Armenia inaugurated the controversial Amulsar gold mine, facing condemnation from environmental groups and activists.
The Economy Minister defended Amulsar for contributing up to 2 percent of GDP and $130m annually, highlighting the conflict with biodiversity goals.
As Armenia seeks closer EU integration, progress on environmental impact assessments, waste management, and air quality should be central.
sum.text:
Its performance is particularly poor on waste management, where it ranks 164th, and wastewater treatment, where it ranks 165th. These figures point to serious shortcomings in basic environmental protection.
The contrast raises an obvious question: why was a country facing such serious environmental challenges chosen to host one of the world’s most important biodiversity conferences? The selection might have offered an opportunity to encourage change, but there is little indication that the Armenian authorities have used the occasion to address the country’s longstanding problems.
A major obstacle is the structure of Armenia’s economy, in which mining plays an important role, alongside ageing industrial facilities and inadequate environmental regulation. The country’s largest mining operations, including the Zangezur, Agarak and Teghut copper-molybdenum mines, extract ore using open-pit methods that generate large quantities of waste and pose serious pollution risks. The World Bank has identified mining as a significant source of environmental pollution in Armenia. Open-pit gold mining has also been licensed at Meghrasar, on land that originally overlapped with Arevik National Park, before the government reduced the park’s boundaries in 2015. The Artsvanik tailings reservoir, which holds millions of tonnes of mining waste, has also been linked to heavy-metal contamination in nearby waterways.
Armenia’s environmental problems extend beyond mining. Forests cover only 11.1 percent of the country, while in Yerevan, levels of harmful fine particle air pollution are about five times the World Health Organization’s recommended limit.
Armenia’s dependence on Russian-linked businesses in some of its most important industrial sectors further complicates efforts to strengthen environmental regulation. These companies are not only major investors and employers, but also important contributors to the state budget, giving the government a powerful economic incentive to protect their operations. Russian-linked investors hold a controlling stake in the Zangezur copper-molybdenum complex, which was Armenia’s largest taxpayer in the first half of 2026.

explain.headline: Odisha CM Accuses Opposition of Selective Memory Regarding Election Commission Independence
static: Article 324 of the Constitution vests the superintendence, direction, and control of elections to Parliament, State Legislatures, and the offices of President and Vice-President in the Election Commission of India.

The Commission originally functioned as a single-member body until October 1989, became multi-member briefly, and was made permanently multi-member from October 1993 with equal decision-making powers.
Under Article 324(5), the Chief Election Commissioner has security of tenure equivalent to a Supreme Court judge and can only be removed through parliamentary impeachment.
Other Election Commissioners cannot be removed from office except on the formal recommendation of the Chief Election Commissioner.

The CEC and Other ECs (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023 established a statutory committee comprising the Prime Minister, a Cabinet Minister, and the Leader of Opposition to appoint Commissioners.
explain.what: The Odisha Chief Minister criticised opposition protests against the Chief Election Commissioner, highlighting past instances of political interference and executive dominance over the Election Commission.
explain.why_in_news: Opposition parties launched protests and filed petitions in the Supreme Court demanding the Chief Election Commissioner step down over voter list revision procedures.
explain.background: Article 324 left appointment methods of Election Commissioners to parliamentary law, which was only codified in 2023 after decades of executive selection.
significance: Highlights the ongoing institutional debates regarding the appointment, tenure protection, and political independence of Election Commissioners.
Brings focus to the distinction between judicial review and political pressure when questioning election administration processes.
Underlines structural reform proposals such as equal constitutional protection against removal for all three Election Commissioners.
prelims: In October 1989, two Election Commissioner posts were first created under Rajiv Gandhi's government.
Sitting CEC N Gopalaswami formally recommended the removal of Election Commissioner Navin Chawla in January 2009.
The 2023 Act mandates a selection committee consisting of the Prime Minister, a Union Cabinet Minister, and the Leader of the Opposition.
A Chief Election Commissioner can only be removed by a motion passed in Parliament by a two-thirds majority.
explain.mains: The institutional independence of the Election Commission of India is vital for electoral integrity. In light of recent controversies, critically evaluate the reforms required in the appointment and removal mechanisms of Election Commissioners.

points: Opposition parties held demonstrations in Delhi seeking the Chief Election Commissioner's resignation without any adverse judicial findings from the Supreme Court.
Protests erupted over the Special Summary Revision (SIR) process, but the author argues the opposition only challenges outcomes where it loses elections.
The core issue is whether current political outrage reflects genuine institutional defense or political opportunism given historical executive interference in election oversight.
In October 1989, the ruling government created two commissioner posts to curtail then CEC Peri Sastri, which were promptly abolished following an electoral defeat.
In October 1993, the government appointed two additional commissioners to dilute the authority of Chief Election Commissioner T N Seshan.
In 2009, sitting CEC N Gopalaswami recommended the removal of Election Commissioner Navin Chawla, but the executive rejected it and promoted Chawla to CEC.
Former CEC T N Seshan later contested presidential elections in 1997 and ran on a Congress ticket against L K Advani in 1999.
The Chief Election Commissioner and Election Commissioners Act 2023 legally established a selection panel that includes the Prime Minister, a Union Minister, and the Leader of the Opposition.
The author argues genuine institutional reform requires granting equal constitutional removal protection to all Commissioners, auditing voter rolls, and recording internal deliberations.
sum.text:
Delhi’s streets have filled with slogans, marches and ultimatums demanding the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner . The script is familiar: The Election Commission was a paragon of independence until yesterday, and a wicked government has just desecrated it.
It is a moving story. It is also a fiction, and those telling it know better.
Begin with what the protesters cannot produce: A finding. The Supreme Court, hearing the pleas on the SIR, declined to pass any interim order suspending the CEC. It issued a notice and asked the Commission to respond. That is all. The Commission rejects the claim that reported objections amount to institutional dissent. A demand for resignation before a single adverse finding is not a legal argument. It is a rally dressed as a verdict.
Article 324 left appointments to the President acting on the government’s advice. Parliament passed no law on the process for more than 70 years, and for most of those decades the Congress party governed. Every Commissioner who served in all that time was the government’s pick. The party that now thunders about capture sat comfortably inside that arrangement for most of its life, and never once felt the urge to fix it.
In October 1989, a month before the general election, Rajiv Gandhi’s government suddenly created two Election Commissioner posts and filled them with S S Dhanoa and V S Seigell. This was widely seen as an attempt to rein in the then CEC, R V S Peri Sastri, with whom the government had fallen out. When Congress lost the election, the new government abolished both posts within weeks. A ruling party facing an umpire it did not trust expanded the commission and left the rest to the voters. That was Congress’s idea of institutional independence.
T N Seshan was no ordinary Commissioner, and his lashings of the political class made him unpopular in the highest circles. The Narasimha Rao government’s reply, in October 1993, was to appoint two more Commissioners, M S Gill and G V G Krishnamurthy. Seshan objected, arguing that it diluted the authority of the Chief Election Commissioner. No one needs to pretend the motive was admiration for his work.
In 2006, L K Advani and more than 200 MPs petitioned President A P J Abdul Kalam to remove Navin Chawla as Election Commissioner for alleged partisanship. China uses panda diplomacy as soft power to project a charming image, while leveraging lucrative commercial rentals and strict political conditions.
The author argues that panda diplomacy embodies manipulation and exploitation, masking China's appropriation of Tibetan geography and wildlife resources.
China charges foreign zoos up to $1.1 million annually per pair, retains ownership of adults and offspring, and charges $600,000 per born cub.
Between 1994 and 2023, China earned nearly $300 million from its panda-rental programme, making the giant panda the most expensive captive species.
Contracts allow China to unilaterally recall pandas for reasons like unauthorised information release, and forbid terms like lease, rental, loan, or contract.
Panda loans historically signal political messaging, such as the 1972 gift after Nixon's visit and recalls following meetings with the Dalai Lama.

sum.text:
During his recent visit to Washington, Chinese President Xi Jinping announced that China would send a breeding pair of giant pandas to Zoo Atlanta. The "envoys of friendship", Ping Ping and Fu Shuang, arrived just a few days later. This is hardly the first time China has used its iconic bear as an instrument of soft power.
By loaning the animals to overseas zoos, it seeks to project an image of China not as a threatening dragon, but rather as a tough but cuddly charmer. But perhaps the true message of this "panda diplomacy" lies in the manipulation and exploitation it embodies. For starters, while China claims the familiar black-and-white bear as its mascot, one of the species' primary natural habitats is Wolong, which sits on the steep edge of the Tibetan Plateau.
Within a horizontal distance of about 30 miles, elevations range from alpine peaks exceeding 17,000 feet to below 1,600 feet, creating a moist, temperate microclimate that sustains the high-altitude bamboo forests where pandas thrive. Historically part of the Tibetan region of Kham, Wolong is now under Sichuan provincial jurisdiction, in Aba Tibetan-Qiang Autonomous Prefecture - nd China is all too eager to subsume everything that makes it culturally unique. Since China's annexation of resource-rich Tibet in 1950-51, the government has systematically sought to erase Tibetan culture and identity, not least by incorporating the Plateau's distinctive geography, wildlife, and natural resources into mainstream Chinese national identity.
China's appropriation of others extends even to cherry-tree cultivation, which it has claimed began not in Japan or Korea, but in "China's Himalayan highlands" - that is, Tibet. The Tibetan Plateau is home to the endangered red panda, a house-cat-sized mammal with a long, bushy tail, in addition to giant pandas, which are classified as a vulnerable species. There are fewer than 2,000 giant pandas left in the wild, and China claims ownership of almost all of them.
This brings us to the second dubious element of China's panda diplomacy: it is based on a lucrative "rent-a-panda-pair" programme. While China reaps the soft-power benefits of keeping its endearing mascot in foreign zoos, it also charges those zoos high prices: up to $1.1 million per year for the right to display and breed a pair of pandas. China retains ownership not only of the leased adults, but also of any offspring they produce.
And yet, the leasing zoo must pay a one-time fee of approximately $600,000…

texts.x: The Supreme Court is right. Linking sex work and trafficking is not always tenable, as it may deny the sex worker her agency

points: The Supreme Court directed magistrates to conduct a mandatory threshold inquiry during anti-trafficking operations to distinguish between voluntary sex work and human trafficking.
This directive seeks to return agency to adult women by inquiring whether they consented to sex work, pushing the State to consider their fundamental right to life and livelihood.
Traditional anti-trafficking raids assume all sex workers are victims of exploitation, leading to detention in care homes, forced medical check-ups, and repatriation.
Linking sex work, trafficking, and coercion is argued to be untenable because it fails to take a woman's consent into account.
Anti-trafficking groups and rescue operations often reinforce the view that all women in sex work are incapable of making choices, which the Supreme Court challenges.
The recent directives issued by Justices JB Pardiwala and R Mahadevan build on the court's May 29 judgment concerning custody and consent.
The apex court previously underscored that sex work in itself is not an offence under the law, meaning voluntarily working adult women cannot be penalised or arrested during raids.
sum.text:
The Supreme Court’s direction to magistrates to conduct a mandatory “threshold inquiry” in the event of an anti-trafficking operation should be seen as more than a mere procedural intervention. The move, which seeks to distinguish between voluntary sex work by an adult woman and human trafficking, returns a woman’s agency back to her. The inquiry, in itself, is not a new thing.
Magistrates have long been tasked with inquiring about a trafficking victim’s details, particularly when ascertaining their age. The significance of the top court’s recent directive, however, lies in the intent behind the inquiry. By seeking to know whether the adult woman has consented to sex work, the court pushes the State to consider her fundamental right to life and livelihood of her choosing.
An anti-trafficking raid on a brothel operates from the assumption that all sex workers are victims of sexual exploitation and coercion, and thus need rescuing. Everything follows from this — the care homes they are sent to, the dismantling of the set-up in which they work, the criminalisation of their networks and clients, the medical check-ups they are subjected to while detained, including ossification tests to determine their age, and their repatriation to their home states. However, to link sex work, trafficking and coercion is untenable, not least because it fails to take the woman’s consent into account, rarely reflecting what’s actually taking place on the ground.
There is already an asymmetry of power in the context in which adult women pursue sex work, and by focussing on their rescue and rehabilitation, anti-trafficking groups reinforce the view that all women in sex work are incapable of making the choice to exit. The top court challenges this infantilisation. The directives issued by the bench of Justices JB Pardiwala and R Mahadevan build on the court’s May 29 judgment, which held that a victim’s consent is also a primary consideration in decisions on long-term custody in a protective home or restoration to her family.
Rehabilitation cannot be imposed against a victim’s will as a matter of routine. The on-ground reality diverges widely from the stereotypes in circulation. Sex work is not a singular kind of work — women operate out of streets, brothels and even their own homes.
Many sex workers have formed unions and groups to advocate for their rights, and to seek State-mandated medical treatment, prophylactics, and access to State-run childcare. Many have, over years,…

explain.headline: AI in Healthcare: Neither Poison Nor Panacea for Doctors
static: Artificial intelligence in healthcare involves the use of machine learning algorithms and software to analyze medical data, assist in diagnostics, and recommend treatments.
Technological solutionism refers to the overestimation of technology as a universal fix for complex social and structural problems, as warned against by the WHO.
Clinical decision support systems are interactive software programs designed to assist physicians and other health professionals with decision-making tasks.
Graded autonomy in AI deployment involves delegating low-risk administrative tasks first while expanding clinical responsibilities only after rigorous safety testing and audits.

explain.why_in_news: Recent studies, including a 2026 Nature report on the AI system MIRA and trials in Kenya, have highlighted the capabilities and limitations of artificial intelligence in medical diagnoses.

Emphasizes data protection, accountability, and validation using domestic patient demographics.
Redefines the core value of human doctors in clinical judgment, empathy, and patient-centric care.

stories.ai_why: Ethical and practical role of AI in healthcare.

texts.x: AI may detect more abnormalities and shorten tasks while expanding care, but automating diagnosis cannot decide whether treatment is affordable or even wanted.

points: Both doctors and patients increasingly consult artificial intelligence tools independently, often unaware of each other's use of the same technology.
A 2026 study in Nature tested an autonomous system named MIRA, showing a diagnostic accuracy of 87.8% compared to 78.1% among physicians.
The primary debate centers on how much care autonomous AI should be permitted to perform and who bears responsibility when harm occurs.
A 2025 US FDA clearance was given to UpDoc, which provides insulin-dose instructions for type-2 diabetes under clinician-set targets and limits.
An analysis of 52 studies revealed that fewer than half of human-AI teams outperformed both working separately, with some performing worse.
A 2026 Kenyan trial showed that AI improved diagnostic accuracy but did not significantly reduce treatment failure rates.
For India, AI offers opportunities to translate health info into local languages, track vital parameters, and extend primary care where specialists are sparse.
India must avoid technological solutionism and ensure graded autonomy, strict data protection, robust accountability, and validation on Indian patient pools.
sum.text:
A doctor checks a prescription with artificial intelligence (AI): Could medicines interact; has anything been missed? At home, their patient asks AI whether the diagnosis is correct and prescribed medicines necessary. A doctor and their patient may consult the same third participant, often unaware of the other’s actions.
Ideally, a “second opinion” should help. But, what happens when AI disagrees with the doctor or with another AI programme? And if its advice causes harm, who is responsible?
The question now is: “How much care should AI be allowed to perform?” An expert article in JAMA predicts autonomous AI may eventually outperform doctors on some cognitive tasks. And a 2026 study published in Nature that tested an autonomous system, MIRA, with simulated electronic health records shows that across 311 cases, AI’s diagnostic accuracy was 87.8% versus 78.1% among physicians. So, there is capability, and the promise of future AI autonomy, but not significant readiness just yet.
The near-term model can be limited autonomy, within clinician-set boundaries. In 2025, the US FDA cleared UpDoc, which provides insulin-dose instructions to adults with type-2 diabetes. Clinicians set targets and limits; the system may withhold advice or direct patients to seek help.
Yet, keeping a doctor in a process does not necessarily produce the best result. An analysis of 52 studies found that clinicians using AI performed seven percentage points better than clinicians alone, but fewer than half of human-AI teams beat both working separately; some did worse. A 2026 Kenyan trial found that AI improved diagnoses but did not significantly reduce treatment failure.
Medicine is more than a likely diagnosis: Illnesses coexist, drugs interact, and patients value different outcomes. There is also a bigger paradox. Dhruv Khullar asks in The New England Journal of Medicine whether AI efficiency will reduce health care workers.
AI may detect more abnormalities and prompt follow-up, shortening tasks while expanding care. Ultimately, automating diagnosis cannot decide whether treatment is affordable, tolerable, or even wanted. What, then, are the opportunities for India?
To begin with, AI in health care could explain health information in familiar languages, track glucose or blood pressure, reduce paperwork, and extend primary care where specialists are sparse. But India must avoid AI-only care for those unable to afford a doctor: WHO, too, warns against “technological solutionism”—…

points: Renewed backchannel diplomacy between Washington and Moscow to explore an armistice has sparked an acute crisis of confidence within the western coalition.
The interceptor dilemma involves the visible throttling of critical Patriot air-defence missile shipments from the US to Kyiv.
American policymakers frame the slowdown as a logistical necessity due to depleted global stockpiles and a need to deter conflicts in other theatres.
Kyiv views the withheld defensive munitions not as a peace incentive, but as a coercive strategy that strips away its civilian shelter.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and the high command warned that Patriot interceptors are running perilously low amid intense Russian missile barrages.

sum.text:
The renewed flurry of backchannel diplomacy between Washington and Moscow has placed the conflict in Ukraine at its most precarious crossroads since the outbreak of hostilities. Behind closed doors, envoys have begun actively probing the parameters of an armistice, exploring the contours of potential territorial freeze-lines, energy infrastructure ceasefires, and future security architectures. Yet, far from fostering battlefield detente, these preliminary overtures have ignited an acute crisis of confidence within the western coalition.
At the epicentre of this diplomatic friction lies what defence analysts now call the interceptor dilemma: The visible throttling and procedural stalling of critical Patriot air-defence missile shipments from the US to Kyiv. What appears in diplomatic circles as calibrated leverage to bring Ukraine to the negotiating table is perceived in Kyiv and across European capitals as a coercive strategy that strips away Ukraine’s civilian shield, exposing its urban power grids and population centres to Russian ballistic devastation on the eve of winter. From the perspective of Washington’s current strategic calculus, the war of attrition has reached an inflection point where indefinite kinetic sustainment collides with global military bandwidth and escalating domestic economic pressures.
American policymakers pushing for exploratory talks argue that uninterrupted escalation risks dragging NATO into an uncontrolled direct confrontation with a nuclear-armed power while consuming precision stockpiles that are urgently needed in other theatres, notably the Indo-Pacific and West Asia. Within this realist framework, diplomacy cannot operate in a vacuum; it requires tangible carrots and sticks applied to both belligerents. By pausing or conditioning offensive strike approvals, scrutinising arms pipelines, and urging Kyiv to halt long-range asymmetric drone strikes against Russian oil refineries to stabilise global energy prices, Washington aims to establish a framework for de-escalation.
For proponents of this pragmatic realism, pacing the transfer of high-end PAC-2 and PAC-3 Patriot interceptors is framed as a logistical necessity born of depleted inventories and worldwide defence industrial bottlenecks, rather than a betrayal of an ally. sum.text:
The government is considering reducing its stake in four public sector banks (PSBs) — Central Bank of India, UCO Bank, Punjab & Sind Bank, and Indian Overseas Bank , to 75% to comply with minimum public shareholding norms, The Economic Times reported. It added that the Centre's immediate priority over the next year is to increase public shareholding in these lenders.
The divestment will likely be done through offers for sale ( OFS ) by the government, depending on market conditions, while the banks could also raise capital from the market based on their individual requirements and strategies. A higher public float is expected to improve the banks' valuations, the report added.
The Centre has long term objective to reduce and combine a number of smaller PSBs down to three to four large corporations, the report added.
In October, the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA) cleared Canadian billionaire Prem Watsa's Fairfax Financial Holdings' acquisition of 60.72% stake in IDBI Bank for ₹ 52,878 crore.
Notably, Union Budget 2022 set a target to privatise two public sector banks and one general insurance company, apart from IDBI Bank .
The Centre is also preparing for another round of consolidation among state-owned lenders, which could include privatising two banks, the ET report said. Earlier, the NITI Aayog had reportedly shortlisted Central Bank of India and Indian Overseas Bank as potential candidates, it added.
However, the government would need legislative amendments to proceed with privatisation. This would include changes to the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, the report said.
Notably, state-owned companies, including financial institutions were exempt from the 25% minimum public shareholding requirement till August 2026 and further extension is expected to be notified, it added.
After the proposed reduction of government stake in the four banks, privatisation would involve transferring control of a bank to a private owner — i.e. similar to IDBI sale to Fairfax.
Notably, the Centre's new Public Sector Enterprise Policy introduced in 2021 classified public sector commercial enterprises into strategic and non-strategic sectors, with provision for all non-strategic sectors PSUs to be considered for privatisation. For strategic sectors, the policy committed retaining a ‘bare minimum presence of the existing public sector commercial enterprises at Holding Company level’.

sum.text:
Newly declassified government documents on UFOs revealed Friday that mysterious black triangle-shaped objects have been spotted moving at speeds up to 1,800 miles per hour without leaving vapor trails over classified US military installations. These sightings occurred on at least three different occasions throughout the past year. Who is behind triangle UFO sightings? These sightings have raised serious national security worries, and according to redacted files on unidentified anomalous phenomena released Friday by the Trump Administration, officials still haven't determined whether these objects originated from foreign nations or elsewhere. The triangle sightings sparked worry for two key reasons: the cutting-edge technology they seemed to display and their location—directly above highly classified US government facilities where experimental technology is developed. For security purposes, the specific locations and dates were kept confidential. Government-released sketches depict the dark, triangle-shaped craft hovering over mountainous terrain. However, no photographs were offered. All on Jasmine Gill's GoFundMe campaign and 8-month-old son.
These enigmatic triangles operated silently, produced no visible exhaust, and when examined using thermal imaging, emitted a steady heat signature—distinctly different from what you'd see with conventional aircraft or drones, which typically show stronger thermal readings in specific areas like their engines. Mysterious triangle objects traveled like ‘fighter jet’, say witnesses.
The object traveled at a velocity that witnesses likened to that of a “fighter jet”, as documented in materials unveiled through the Trump administration's Presidential Unsealing and Reporting System for UAP Encounters initiative.“The exterior presented as a continuous (seamless), featureless surface lacking any discernible structural discontinuities, propulsive apertures, intake structures, aerodynamic control effectors, or cockpit features,” a Department of War memo mentioned about a different triangle sighting. According to the memo, both primary witnesses experienced no physical health impacts, with no documented cases of disorientation, nausea, headaches, memory loss, or any other unusual sensory experiences. Friday's release represented the seventh batch of documents disclosed to the public, and government officials said during Thursday's briefing with reporters that additional releases are planned.

sum.text:
New Delhi, Oct 24 (PTI) The Centre has created 11 crore unique 11-digit Farmer IDs, or Kisan Pehchaan Patra, under the AgriStack framework, five months ahead of the March 2027 deadline, Union Agriculture Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan said on Saturday.
These identification numbers are being issued as part of the Digital Agriculture Mission.
In a video message, Chouhan said the milestone was achieved on the night of October 23. "The task of creating 11 crore Farmer IDs has been completed ahead of schedule," he said.
Calling it a "historic day for Indian agriculture", the minister said Prime Minister Narendra Modi had set the target of 11 crore IDs by March 2027. He linked the effort to the government's vision of a "Viksit Bharat", saying a modern agricultural sector would require the use of technology.
The Farmer ID, Chouhan said, is meant to ensure that the benefits of government schemes reach the right farmers at the right time and transparently. "There will no longer be a need to repeatedly submit piles of paperwork or provide endless documentation," he said.
According to the minister, the ID will be the only document a farmer needs to access bank loans, crop insurance, disaster relief and to sell produce.
Chouhan thanked officials and staff of the Central government, as well as state governments, Union Territories and district administrations, for the achievement.
Addressing farmers directly, he said they now had "their own unique identity" and urged them to take timely advantage of government schemes and adopt technology to improve farming practices. PTI LUX DRR

New Delhi, Oct 24 (IANS) The Viksit Bharat - Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) (VB-G RAM G) has recorded strong progress across multiple implementation metrics with active workers numbering 10.88 crore in 2026-27 and assets created totalling 2.83 lakh, an official statement said on Saturday.
Person‑days generated exceeded 31.69 crore, while women’s participation stood at 61.65 per cent. Employment was provided on demand to over 2.81 crore workers from about 2.23 crore rural households and around 97.17 lakh workers are currently under execution.
“VB-G RAM G brings employment, participatory planning and rural development together. Through VGPPs, Gram Panchayats identify local needs, map existing assets and prioritise development works,” the statement said.
Technology, convergence and digital systems strengthen implementation, transparency and accountability. The framework links employment with sustainable asset creation, supporting resilient livelihoods and integrated rural development.
The statement said 73.24 lakh approved works are readily available to meet future employment demand and about 20.16 lakh active worksites are operational.
Nearly 2.31 lakh Gram Panchayats are executing works across the country, and 3.76 crore direct benefit transfer transactions have been recorded in 2026‑27.
Wage rates range from Rs 300 to Rs 450 per day and 15.17 crore Gramin Rozgar Guarantee Cards have been issued.
The transition from Mahatma Gandhi NREGA to VB-G RAM G has been seamless and disruption-free, the statement said, adding that digital systems supporting implementation were operational from the commencement of the new framework.
VB-G RAM G Act, 2025 provides a statutory guarantee of 125 days of wage employment every financial year. The guarantee covers every rural household whose adult members volunteer for unskilled manual work. It promotes empowerment, growth, convergence and saturation for a prosperous and resilient rural Bharat.

sum.text:
The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) is gearing up to launch the GSLV-F18 mission carrying the NVS-03 navigation satellite on October 30, 2026, from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre. This upcoming mission marks a critical milestone for India's regional GPS alternative, Navigation with Indian Constellation (NavIC). Due to the natural aging of older spacecraft and critical atomic clock failures, the indigenous navigation system has dropped below its required standalone strength.
While it currently provides basic timing services, it lacks the four operational satellites needed to determine independent positioning data. The NVS-03 launch is specifically intended to restore this location-tracking autonomy." The upcoming launch is of vital significance given the current geopolitical landscape and our push toward regional self-reliance," an ISRO official noted. "NVS-03 will successfully add advanced capabilities, including civilian L1 band compatibility for mass consumer markets and heightened signal security for authorized users." Weighing roughly 2,232 kilograms, the state-of-the-art satellite will be deployed into a Geosynchronous Transfer Orbit (GTO) using the GSLV Mk II rocket.

sum.text:
PLFS Revamp Latest News The Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) is revamping the Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) to improve the measurement of emerging forms of employment and unpaid work. The revised design will be implemented from January 2027, and the proposed changes seek to better capture digital platform workers, unpaid household and caregiving work, volunteer activities and unpaid trainee work. The move is significant because conventional employment statistics can understate the contribution of workers engaged in informal, platform-based and non-market activities, particularly women’s unpaid work.
Better Coverage of Gig and Platform Workers Creating a separate sampling stratum: MoSPI had begun collecting information on digital platform workers experimentally from January 2026. However, the existing sampling arrangement did not identify sufficient platform workers. The revised PLFS will create a separate Second Stage Stratum (SSS) for households containing digital platform workers, thereby improving their representation in the sample.
An additional yes/no screening question will ask whether any household member worked through a digital platform during the preceding 365 days. Platforms mentioned include Ola, Uber, Zomato, Amazon and Urban Company. The information will help identify households eligible for inclusion in the new platform-worker stratum.
Understanding the nature of platform work: Identified platform workers will be asked about the goods or services provided; whether they work for multiple platforms; reasons for entering platform work; and major challenges faced. These challenges may include long working hours, harsh weather conditions, uncertain earnings, accident-related risks and inadequate social security. The data can help policymakers design appropriate labour protection, social-security and income-security mechanisms for the growing platform economy.
Why it matters: A NITI Aayog estimate put Indias gig and platform workforce at 77 lakh in 2020–21, projected to reach 2.35 crore by 2029–30. Better data is therefore essential for evidence-based policymaking. Beyond Conventional Employment Statistics The revised PLFS will collect information on own-use production, unpaid household and caregiving activities, volunteer work and unpaid trainee work.
Questions will cover activities such as fetching water; cooking and cleaning; washing clothes; feeding and caring for children; caring for elderly family members;…

sum.text:
Supreme Court Withdraws Report RequirementThe Supreme Court has withdrawn its direction requiring trial and high courts to call for reports on aggravating and mitigating circumstances in every case involving an offence punishable with death, acknowledging that the exercise could prove unworkable in cases where the court does not even contemplate imposing capital punishment. A three-judge bench of justices Vikram Nath, Sandeep Mehta and Aparesh Kumar Singh accepted a clarification plea by the National Legal Services Authority (NALSA) and deleted a key direction issued by the court on April 27, 2026, which had sought to institutionalise a comprehensive assessment of the circumstances surrounding both the crime and the offender before sentencing. The court agreed with NALSA’s submission that requiring trial courts to obtain such reports in every death-eligible case could create procedural difficulties, particularly since they might not have the resources or facilities to undertake the extensive exercise.
It also recognised that many such cases may not lead the trial court to consider a death sentence at all.“Having considered the submissions advanced, we are in agreement with the submission of Ms. Rashmi Nandakumar (NALSA’s counsel),” said the bench in its recent order, directing deletion of the impugned paragraph and ordering that a corrigendum be issued and the corrected order circulated to all concerned. Other Directions Remain in PlaceThe April order had required trial and high courts to call for reports on aggravating and mitigating circumstances as a matter of course once an accused was convicted, before determining the sentence. The direction was part of a wider set of measures aimed at ensuring that courts had a complete picture of the convict’s background and prospects of reform before deciding whether the death penalty was warranted.
To be sure, the latest order, passed in a murder case from Bihar, does not delete the separate direction requiring high courts to call for such reports at the admission stage of a death reference if they have not been obtained or placed on record by the trial court. The other directions concerning comprehensive reports, dedicated legal teams for death-penalty cases and mitigation investigations also remain in place. sum.text: The Supreme Court has directed the Rajasthan government to seal and dismantle all illegal discharge points into the Jojari-Luni-Bandi river system and recover environmental compensation from polluters for the entire period of violations, while calling for a shift from a reactive to a proactive approach to tackling environmental damage. The directions form part of suo motu proceedings initiated by the court last year after a news report highlighted alarming levels of pollution in the Jojari river, which serves as a lifeline for a population of 2 million in the state. In its order issued on September 29 and uploaded recently, the court directed the state government to “seal and dismantle” all illegal and unauthorised discharge points into the river, including bypass arrangements, manholes, chambers, pipelines and conduits. The concerned state authorities were also directed to initiate appropriate proceedings against the landowners or occupiers and state officials responsible for the lapses. The order further directed the Rajasthan State Pollution Control Board (RSPCB) to “initiate proceedings for assessment, imposition and actual recovery of Environmental Compensation” for the entire period of the violations from the industrial units, persons or entities that benefited from them. The court said environmental issues did not merit an incident-based response in which the state bureaucracy reacts only after a violation is reported. It called for a “fundamental shift” in the approach, requiring the state machinery to anticipate potential environmental risks and act proactively. The bench of justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta said, “There is a dire need for a fundamental change in the manner in which the bureaucracy approaches these issues.” It added, “The state machinery must shed its traditional reactive posture, move away from a practice of responding only after violations are brought to its notice, and bring about an internal reorientation in its functioning so as to anticipate environmental risks, act proactively and ensure continuous coordination amongst the concerned authorities.” The latest order is part of a series of directions issued by the court over the past few months to halt industrial activities along the three rivers, strengthen common effluent treatment plants (CETPs) and prevent industrial waste from being discharged directly into the river system. points: Central Bank of India reported that Rs 13.97 crore was siphoned from its settlement account with the RBI.
The siphoning occurred through 187 unauthorised transfers executed between October 15 and 17.
The bank alleges that unknown persons breached the central SFMS server of Iftas using the core banking system's SFMS server.
The stolen funds were diverted into 36 different bank accounts as per the FIR registered at the Nodal Cyber Police Station in Mumbai.
A total of 6 transfers occurred on October 15, 88 on October 16, and 93 on October 17.
The bank's internal team failed to find any of these 187 transactions in branches, mobile banking, internet banking, or core systems.

sum.text:
Central Bank of India has told the police that ₹13.97 crore was siphoned from its settlement account with the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) through 187 unauthorised transfers between October 15 and 17. The bank alleges that unknown persons got into the central SFMS server of Indian Financial Technology and Allied Services (Iftas), a wholly owned RBI subsidiary, through the SFMS server of its core banking system. SFMS, the Structured Financial Messaging System, carries the payment messages that banks exchange through the RBI’s RTGS and NEFT systems. The money went into 36 bank accounts, according to the first information report (FIR) registered at the Nodal Cyber Police Station, Mumbai. The complainant is the bank’s general manager (treasury). Six transfers were made on October 15, 88 on October 16 and 93 on October 17, the FIR stated. According to the complaint, the bank’s internal team could not find any of the 187 transactions in any branch, in internet or mobile banking, or through any other channel. Consumer panel directs Central Bank to refund ₹95k to ex-stafferNor could it find them in its core banking system, its RTGS settlement account or the SFMS server. Partial traces of 10 of the accounts appear in SFMS database logs, the complaint stated, but the transaction IDs do not appear in the bank’s records. A police officer, who asked not to be named, said little was known about the transactions, making it “very difficult to find how the money was siphoned off”.The complaint says the accounts named as payers in the 187 transactions do not belong to Central Bank of India. The bank maintains a settlement account with the RBI and a separate RTGS settlement account, and its system has an RTGS portal for such payments, the officer said. Sitharaman urges regulators to speed up refunds of unclaimed bank deposits, shares and funds.
In a normal RTGS payment, the complaint stated, the bank enters the customer’s slip in its core banking system and debits the customer’s account. The amount is credited to the bank’s RTGS settlement account. A message then goes from the bank’s SFMS server to Iftas’s central SFMS server, and the amount is debited from the bank’s settlement account with the RBI.The complaint alleges that unknown persons gained unauthorised access to Iftas’s central SFMS through the SFMS server of the bank’s core banking system, and diverted the money from the bank’s account with the RBI.It says the fraud cheated the bank and the members of the public…

points: The International Monetary Fund raised India's FY27 growth forecast from 6.4 percent to 7 percent, driven by better-than-expected economic performance.
The primary trigger for caution is an energy crisis caused by disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz that shows no signs of easing.
The core risk highlighted by the IMF is the potential confluence of multiple shocks coming together to weigh on regional and Indian growth.
Specific risks include a weakening rupee, rising borrowing costs, uncertainty surrounding the artificial intelligence boom, and the threat of El Nino.
The IMF Asia chief warned that prolonged energy shocks could fuel domestic inflation, weaken external balances, and erode household purchasing power.
Central banks are advised to remain agile and keep price stability as their primary objective while responding proactively to price pressures.
Fiscal buffers across the region are thinning due to back-to-back shocks, leaving limited room to absorb higher energy import costs.
The IMF recommended long-term strategies such as diversifying energy sources, reducing fossil fuel dependence, and carrying out domestic land and labour reforms.
sum.text:
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has raised India's FY27 growth forecast to 7% from 6.4%, offering reason for optimism, but the road ahead is far from free of risks.
An energy crisis triggered by disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz that shows no signs of easing, a rupee under pressure, rising borrowing costs, uncertainty over the AI boom and the threat of El Nino could all complicate India's growth outlook. But, the real danger, IMF Asia chief Krishna Srinivasan said, is when these risks converge.
"The biggest worry is if all of these come together, the confluence of risks come together, that can have a significant bearing on prospects for India and for the region," Krishna Srinivasan, Director of the IMF's Asia and Pacific Department said in an exclusive interview with India Today.
The IMF revised its forecast after India's economic performance in FY26-27 exceeded expectations, with the Fund projecting medium-term growth at around 6.9%.
However, Srinivasan cautioned that sustaining this momentum would depend on how India navigates mounting global uncertainties, particularly the prolonged energy shock and its impact on inflation and growth.
"The energy shock is likely to get worse before it gets better," Srinivasan added.
For India, which relies heavily on imported energy, a prolonged disruption could fuel domestic inflation, weaken external balances and weigh on growth. Higher energy costs can erode household purchasing power, raise production expenses for businesses and complicate the task of containing inflation.
At the same time, allowing inflation to remain elevated can undermine growth over the longer term.
Srinivasan said central banks must respond proactively to rising price pressures, with price stability remaining their primary objective.
"The overarching objective of central banks should be on price stability," he said, adding that policymakers must remain agile as inflationary pressures build.
The IMF Asia chief also highlighted the pressure on Asia, which remains heavily dependent on imported oil and gas, with energy consumption accounting for around 4% of the region's GDP, roughly twice the share in the European Union.
India has already diversified its energy import sources, Srinivasan noted. But the room to absorb higher costs through fiscal measures is not unlimited.
"Fiscal buffers are thinning, not just in India, but across the region, because of the shocks we've had back to back," he said.

The Maharashtra Cabinet announced the Fodder Development Policy on 29 September 2026.

The Maharashtra policy sets district-wise plans for cultivating grasses, fodder trees and improved fodder crops. It proposes adding 331.42 thousand hectares to the area under fodder cultivation over five years. The policy provides for using land managed by the Forest and Revenue Departments for fodder cultivation. Some land is to be leased to women’s self-help groups. The government also plans to distribute fodder seeds through a ₹62 crore fund, encourage cultivation by farmers with assured water sources and procure fodder at a guaranteed price.

On 18 October, Latur district, where all 10 talukas were drought-affected, prohibited the use of crop residue as industrial fuel and restricted fodder sales and transport outside the district. New Delhi: External Affairs Minister (EAM) S Jaishankar on Saturday hosted Heads of Mission from African countries, with discussions focusing on various aspects of the India-Africa partnership, the rise of Africa in a multipolar world and new possibilities for people-centric cooperation.“Delighted to host Heads of Mission from Africa this afternoon. The India-Africa partnership is one of shared histories, common aspirations and Deep South-South solidarity. We discussed its different aspects, the rise of Africa in a multipolar world and new possibilities for our people-centric cooperation,” EAM Jaishankar posted on X.Earlier this month, EAM Jaishankar chaired a conference of India’s Heads of Mission in Africa in Addis Ababa, saying India and Africa share deep linkages built upon Global South solidarity, strategic autonomy, multipolarity and common development aspirations.“We held in-depth discussions on taking forward our partnership across trade, investments, connectivity, development partnership, and capacity building,” he had said.
The conference came a day after the EAM laid out his vision for the India-Africa partnership in an address in the Ethiopian capital, where he said partnerships of the future must “help create capabilities, not promote dependencies”, and called for a reformed UN Security Council with fair representation for Africa.“It is no longer sufficient to describe India and Africa only through the vocabulary of historical solidarity. History has given us trust,” EAM Jaishankar had said, stressing that the relationship must now evolve. He said development partnerships could be built on mutual respect.“They need not be prescriptive, condescending or conditional.
They can be based on respect and equality, shared capabilities, and most of all, shared prosperity,” he said. On global governance, EAM Jaishankar said India worked resolutely during its G20 Presidency in 2023 to secure permanent membership for the African Union, and “the same logic now applies to the reform process of the UN Security Council”.

NEW DELHI: The Enforcement Directorate (ED) has moved the Supreme Court challenging the Delhi high court’s order quashing a money laundering case against news portal NewsClick and its editor-in-chief, Prabir Purkayastha, over alleged violations of foreign direct investment (FDI) rules. The ED argued that the high court quashed its Enforcement Case Information Report (ECIR) without examining the merits of the case under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA). It also flagged a five-month delay in the pronouncement of the judgment. The matter is yet to be listed for hearing. Why Delhi HC quashed ED's case against NewsClickIn a judgment dated May 29, Justice Neena Bansal Krishna of the Delhi high court described the continuation of an FIR registered by the Delhi Police’s Economic Offences Wing (EOW) as “nothing but a gross abuse of the process of law”. The judge held that quashing the FIR for the predicate offence also warranted the closure of the ED’s ECIR. Gross abuse of law’: Delhi HC quashes FIR, ED case against Newsclick, founder.
The court ruled that the investment was an "economic decision that did not spell out any criminal offence”. Citing the Union ministry of information and broadcasting’s reply to NewsClick, Justice Krishna noted there was no cap or restriction on FDI in digital media at the time. The single-judge bench ruled that the investment followed acceptable practices and that the allegations, even if accepted, did not establish cheating or criminal breach of trust. The alleged victim in the cheating case should have been M/s Worldwide Media Holdings LLC, but the company had filed no complaint. Instead, the complaint came from “merely an informant”.Justice Krishna also rejected the fund-siphoning allegation, noting that a digital media company would naturally incur expenses on salaries, consultation fees and rent. static: Article 324 of the Constitution vests the superintendence, direction, and control of elections to Parliament, State Legislatures, and the offices of President and Vice-President in the Election Commission.

points: A public interest litigation was filed in the Supreme Court seeking an independent expert committee to examine institutional shortcomings in the Election Commission of India.
The petition follows reports that two Election Commissioners recorded written objections on 14 occasions regarding unilateral decisions by the Chief Election Commissioner.
At stake is the internal governance, collegiate decision-making, and technical integrity of India's apex election management body.
The petitioner also sought an absolute prohibition on election campaigning using religious tags, communal appeals, sectarian identity, or hate speech.
Dissenting notes reportedly involved unauthorized alterations to statutory Form 6, electoral database centralization, work allocation, and West Bengal appeal filings.
The plea highlighted that in West Bengal, out of 38.20 lakh voter exclusion appeals, only 1.02 lakh were disposed of.
The proposed committee would be chaired by a former Chief Justice of India and include specialists in law, technology, statistics, and cybersecurity.
The Supreme Court's response will determine whether judicial oversight will be instituted to scrutinize the Election Commission's internal processes and data management.
sum.text:
A public interest litigation (PIL) petition has been filed before the Supreme Court seeking constitution of an independent expert committee, chaired by a former Chief Justice of India or a former judge of the top court, to examine institutional shortcomings in the functioning of the Election Commission of India (ECI)..The plea, filed by advocate Vishal Tiwari, has also sought directions to the ECI to enforce an "absolute prohibition" on election campaigning using religious tags, religious symbols, communal appeals, sectarian identity or hate speech..The petition states that it is intended to be non-partisan and prospective and that the petitioner is not seeking a finding against any political party or office-holder, nor does it challenge the result of any election. It relies on a September 23 report by The Indian Express that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had recorded written objections on at least 14 occasions over ten months regarding unilateral decisions taken by Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar..As per the petition, these objections pertained to unauthorized alterations to statutory Form 6, centralisation of the electoral database, unapproved appeal filings in West Bengal, and work allocation orders. The ECI, the plea says, acknowledged the dissenting notes but described them as routine suggestions, without clarifying who authorised the changes to Form 6..The plea has also flagged the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls in West Bengal.
Citing media reports of an ECI affidavit, it states that approximately 38.20 lakh appeals had been filed by persons excluded from electoral rolls of which only around 1.02 lakh have been disposed off. The ECI reportedly sought an increase in appellate tribunals from 19 to 42. Another report cited in the plea states that 2,70,313 electors in Maharashtra's draft electoral roll were shown as aged between 101 and 150 years due to a default birth year glitch..Hence, the ECI's shortcomings should be examined by a committee of experts.
The proposed committee, as per the plea, should include experts in constitutional law, election administration, statistics, technology, cybersecurity and data protection.

The National Industrial Corridor Development Corporation (NICDC) marked a significant milestone in advancing industrial development in Bihar with the formal launch of Bihar Integrated Manufacturing City Gaya Limited (BIMCGL) by the Chief Minister of Bihar, Shri Samrat Choudhary, at Bodh Gaya, the release said. Spread across 1,670 acres in the Dobhi block of Gaya district, the project was approved by the Centre on August 28, 2024, at a total cost of Rs 1,339 crore, including land acquisition costs. It is expected to attract investments of approximately Rs 16,500 crore and generate employment opportunities for around 1.10 lakh people, the release said. Incorporated on January 6, 2025, BIMCGL is a joint venture between the Bihar Industrial Area Development Authority (BIADA) and the National Industrial Corridor Development and Implementation Trust (NICDIT), with both holding equal equity stakes. As the dedicated implementing agency, BIMCGL will expedite project execution through coordinated planning, infrastructure development, statutory clearances, utility connectivity and investor facilitation, the Ministry said, adding, The institutional framework will enable faster decision-making, effective monitoring and timely resolution of implementation-related issues. Infrastructure development at IMC Gaya is underway, with the Bihar government taking possession of the entire project land. The Centre released the first equity tranche of Rs 132 crore in September 2025 against the transfer of 415 acres. Project management consultants and an EPC contractor for trunk infrastructure works have been appointed, while physical construction has commenced. Construction of a dedicated helipad at IMC Gaya is also at an advanced stage to improve accessibility for investors, business delegations and senior officials. Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Russian President Vladimir Putin have directed their governments to expand bilateral cooperation as the two countries work towards increasing trade to USD 100 billion by 2030, Indian Ambassador to Russia Vinay Kumar told the Press Trust of India. The two leaders discussed the full range of bilateral relations on the sidelines of the BRICS summit in New Delhi on September 12 and 13, Kumar said in an interview with Russian news agency TASS published on Saturday.“One of the concrete results of the cooperation was the joint participation of the leaders of our countries in the BRICS business summit, as well as a visit to the Innoprom-India exhibition — the first Russian industrial exhibition held in New Delhi,” Kumar told TASS.He said the leaders had directed the relevant ministries and agencies to further develop cooperation, including in trade and commerce. India and Russia continued to work towards increasing bilateral trade to USD 100 billion and two-way investment to USD 50 billion by 2030, Kumar said.
On labour cooperation, the ambassador said India aimed to provide Russia with the required number of skilled workers in line with its needs. Indians account for around 25 to 30 per cent of Russia's quota for foreign workers, he added. Kumar said India, with a population of nearly 1.5 billion, was set to become a global centre for skilled personnel.
The average age of India's workforce is 29 years, while workers account for about 69 per cent of the population, he said. India trains specialists for its domestic market as well as for jobs overseas, Kumar said. New Delhi had proposed that Russia set up educational institutions in India or collaborate with existing Indian institutions to train workers required by Russian industries, he added.
India and Russia are therefore focusing on expanding trade, investment and labour cooperation, with their governments tasked with taking forward the decisions made by Modi and Putin.

sum.text:
New Delhi, Oct 24: Union Minister of State for Science and Technology, Dr Jitendra Singh, on Saturday inaugurated an integrated air pollution analysis facility in Delhi-NCR that can identify pollution sources in real time and assess the chemical composition and potential toxicity of pollutants.
The facility, named the Integrated Atmospheric Chemistry and Aerosol Toxicity Analysis Laboratory (AATAL), has been established at the Delhi branch of the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology (IITM) under Mission Mausam.
Describing it as a first-of-its-kind facility globally, Dr Jitendra Singh said it would help authorities move beyond measuring pollution levels to understanding the sources, composition and health implications of pollutants. “Earlier, the discussion would largely revolve around whether the pollution level was 100 or 200. This facility will help us understand the composition of pollution as well as the contribution of different sources,” he said.
The laboratory will help scientists distinguish between pollution caused by vehicles, industries, biomass and crop-residue burning, construction activities, road dust and pollutants transported from neighbouring regions.
During a media interaction, Dr Jitendra Singh cited a real-time assessment displayed on a screen, which showed transport contributing around 25 per cent of Delhi’s air pollution, with the overall pollution level at approximately 180. He said such information would help authorities take targeted measures based on the actual sources of pollution.
Equipped with advanced instruments, AATAL will analyse fine particulate matter (PM2.5), atmospheric gases, metals, toxic elements and other pollutants to help scientists understand their composition and potential health effects.
The facility is integrated with IITM’s AIRWISE (Air Quality Warning and Integrated Decision Support System for Emissions), which combines air-quality observations, forecasts and pollution-source information. The system provides forecasts for the next 72 hours at a spatial resolution of 400 metres, enabling pollution levels and their likely sources to be assessed across different parts of Delhi.
Dr Jitendra Singh said the initiative reflected a coordinated approach involving scientific institutions, environmental authorities and pollution-control agencies to address air pollution.
Dr Sachin Ghude, Project Director, MAQWS, said the facility would provide scientific evidence to the Commission for Air Quality Management…

sum.text:
Hampi (Vijayanagara): A Unesco-ICOMOS reactive monitoring mission arrived in Hampi on Saturday afternoon to inspect heritage monuments and review conservation measures, tourism infrastructure and development plans for the World Heritage site until Oct 27. The delegation comprises international heritage experts George Abungu from Kenya and Ichida Shimoda from Japan, and Archaeological Survey of India additional director general Jahnavi Sharma. Deputy commissioner and Hampi World Heritage Area Management Authority chairperson Kavitha S Mannikeri said the team would examine monument conservation measures, future regulations and tourist facilities.

sum.text:
Zuqar Island Latest News Yemen’s Houthi rebels recently claimed they are attempting to rescue a boat carrying 14 Indian nationals near Zuqar Island in the Red Sea, alleging that it was targeted by Saudi Arabia. About Zuqar Island It is a Yemeni island in the southern Red Sea, forming part of the Hanish Islands archipelago. It lies between the coasts of mainland Yemen and Eritrea, near the Bab-el-Mandeb strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.
Despite its proximity to the African continent, the island is considered a part of Asia because it sits on the Asian continental shelf. It has strategic importance because of its location along one of the world’s key maritime routes. Eritrea captured the island in 1995 after battling Yemeni forces.
An international court in 1998 placed the island formally into Yemen’s custody. The island consists of a shield volcano overlain by basaltic pyroclastic cones and spatter cones, which produce youthful-looking pahoehoe lava flows. Several small coastal cones and islets surrounding Zuqar Island were formed by phreatic eruptions.
Pahoehoe is a type of basaltic lava characterized by a smooth, often shiny, and billowy surface. This highly fluid lava spreads in thin sheets and forms ropy folds as it continues to flow beneath a hardening crust. The surface of pahoehoe lava flows can appear gently undulating or broadly hummocky, with liquid lava beneath the surface wrinkling it into tapestry-like folds that resemble twisted rope.
These flows are typically fed internally by streams of liquid lava.

points: More than 3,500 sal, bija and tendu trees in the Karka landscape of Udanti-Sitanadi Tiger Reserve have been found damaged by deliberate ring-barking.
Girdling removes bark around the trunk and interrupts nutrient transport, causing trees to slowly die so encroached land can be opened up.
Encroachment in the area expanded from 22 hectares in 2016 to 102.47 hectares in 2026, quadrupling in a decade.
A drone survey combined with ISRO satellite imagery indicates more than 1.25 lakh trees may have been cleared between 2016 and 2026.
Conservationist Vijay Nishanth and grafting specialists from Raipur are using liquid treatments, protective coverings and bridge grafting to save the wounded trees.
Bridge grafting uses living tissue to span the girdled portion, helping resume nutrient flow between the roots and upper trunk.
USTR previously experimented with bridge grafting in the Tourenga range in 2022, achieving a success rate of only around 10%.
The operation also trains local forest guards and field staff to assess injuries, perform grafting, and monitor trees over time.
The Karka forest links to the origins of the Mahanadi and supports tigers, elephants, Indian giant squirrels, and Malabar pied hornbills.
sum.text:
Raipur: In a forest where thousands of trees were deliberately ring-barked and left to slowly die, an unusual rescue operation has begun: liquid medicines, moisture-retaining material, tree “band-aids” and bridge grafts are being used to try to bring them back to life. More than 3,500 sal, bija and tendu trees in the Karka landscape of Udanti-Sitanadi Tiger Reserve (USTR) have been found damaged by girdling — removal of bark around the trunk, which interrupts the tree’s nutrient transport system and can eventually kill it. Karnataka-based conservationist Vijay Nishanth, popularly known as a “tree doctor”, has reached the reserve and begun assessing and treating the injured trees with forest staff. Grafting specialists from Raipur have also been roped in for the operation, while material brought to the site includes liquid treatment formulations, moisture retainers and protective coverings for exposed wounds. What has given the team some hope is that not every wounded tree has waited for human intervention. Officials observed that a few had begun naturally healing damaged portions of their bark, indicating that at least some of the trees may still have sufficient vitality to recover if protected and treated in time. A forest injured to make way for encroachment.
The rescue is unfolding against a much larger story of forest loss in Karka. Encroachment in the area has expanded from 22 hectares in 2016 to 102.47 hectares in 2026, more than quadrupling in a decade. A TOI had reported recently that a DGPS-enabled drone survey assessed alongside ISRO satellite imagery indicates that more than 1.25 lakh trees may have been cleared from the affected landscape between 2016 and 2026, according to USTR.Field inspections found trees with both old and fresh girdling wounds, raising concern within the forest department that standing trees were being deliberately weakened so they would eventually die and the land could be opened up further, said Varun Jain, deputy director of UTSR.Unlike felling, girdling can leave a tree standing for months or even years while it gradually loses its ability to sustain itself. First, doctors decide which trees can survive.
The treatment is not uniform. Teams are first examining the depth and age of each injury and whether enough living tissue remains for the tree to recover. points: The Railway Board extended the optional travel insurance facility to passengers booking reserved tickets offline at railway counters following a Supreme Court order.
The board directed all railway zones to implement the counter insurance facility by October 27, ensuring staff inform passengers about it.
The core issue involves bridging the welfare gap for passengers from remote areas who rely on offline counters rather than online booking.
The insurance premium for counter tickets is fixed at 45 paise per ticket, matching the e-ticket premium rate.
The payment of the insurance premium must be done exclusively through digital means at the reservation counters.
Reservation staff must accurately capture a mandatory mobile number and passenger particulars to transmit details to the insurance company.
Policy details will be communicated to the opted passengers through their registered mobile numbers under existing IRCTC guidelines.
The sum insured ranges from Rs 2 lakh to Rs 10 lakh depending on the severity of the death, disability, or injury.
sum.text:
FOLLOWING THE Supreme Court order, the Railway Board has extended the optional travel insurance facility to passengers booking reserved tickets through offline mode or from railway counters. Earlier, the facility was available only for reserved tickets booked online.
The board on Saturday directed all railway zones to ensure the facility at railway counters by October 27, as ordered by the top court, and also asked the staff to inform the passengers about its implementation.
According to existing IRCTC guidelines, the scheme applies only to Indian citizens and is provided only for confirmed, partly confirmed, and RAC (Reservation Against Cancellation) tickets at the time of booking.
The passengers will be charged 45 paise premium per counter ticket, the same as the e-ticket premium. The payment of the premium will be done digitally only.
“Where a passenger opts for insurance, the applicable premium shall be collected along with the ticket fare through digital means only… Reservation staff shall ensure that the mobile number (mandatory) along with requisite passenger particulars are captured accurately in accordance with the prescribed reservation procedure, so as to facilitate transmission of the relevant details to the insurance company for issuance of the policy,” said the Board.
It further said adequate instructions shall be issued to reservation supervisors and counter staff. Passengers opting for insurance shall be informed that the policy details will be communicated through their registered mobile number.
The existing terms and conditions of Optional Travel Insurance Scheme (OTIS) for e-ticket passengers, as issued by IRCTC, will be equally applicable to insurance policies issued for tickets purchased through counters.
In an order dated October 6, the SC ordered the Railway Board to extend the insurance facility to offline or counter tickets. Though over 87% of the railway tickets are booked online, a lot of passengers coming from remote areas still rely on counter tickets for travel.
“Court has granted sufficient time to the authorities to devise a mechanism for extending such coverage to persons belonging to the lowest strata of society, who, in most cases, purchase their tickets at the railway reservation counters while undertaking journeys by train,” said the top court.
Travel insurance is necessary for passengers to get compensation in the wake of train accidents and any untoward incidents leading to deaths and injuries. While the Railways has…
